extracted.intended_audience: general readers and aspiring poets/writers (readers of literary memoirs and creative-writing practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and memoir-observations about choosing a unifying subject for a long poem and practical matters of producing/publishing periodical prose/poetry. Emphasises subject choice, structural unity, working from immediate observation, and audience/market considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication format, frequency, and pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: The work was to be published on every eighth day, thirty-two pages, large octavo, closely printed, and price only four-pence (in order to exempt it from the stamp-tax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies concrete production parameters (frequency, pagecount, size, close type) and price used to meet legal/tax constraints and market positioning; also implies that these choices affect audience acceptance and financial viability. Includes example that delays in publication and inappropriate content led to subscriber loss and financial difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject that supplies natural connection and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I had considered it as a defect in the admirable poem of THE TASK, that the subject, which gives the title to the work, was not, and indeed could not be, carried on beyond the three or four first pages... I sought for a subject, that should give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society, yet supply in itself a natural connection to the parts, and unity to the whole.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning a long poem, select a subject that inherently links its parts and permits varied modes (description, incident, reflection). Example given: tracing a stream from source to sea as a subject that provides continuous, unifying material and allows transitions between scenes and reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward connections and abrupt transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticises a work for having connections frequently awkward, and the transitions abrupt and arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural coherence and smooth transitions between sections are essential for long-form poetry; aim for natural, principle-driven links rather than jolting or arbitrary shifts. This is cited as a concrete defect to be remedied by better subject choice and planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from direct observation and make studies
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘My walks therefore were almost daily on the top of Quantock, and among its sloping coombes. With my pencil and memorandum-book in my hand, I was making studies... and often moulding my thoughts into verse, with the objects and imagery immediately before my senses.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use on-site observation, sketches, and notes as raw material for verse: composing with imagery and objects immediately before the senses improves descriptive richness and grounded detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience and anticipate political/religious sensitivities
rubrics_metrics.description: An essay against fast days with a censurable application of a text from Isaiah lost the author near five hundred subscribers at one blow; subsequent issues alienated patrons by unexpected targets and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing politically or religiously charged content (especially for a subscription/periodical audience), be mindful of readers’ expectations and sensitivities. Tone, choice of targets, and unexpected departures from promised stance or motto can rapidly erode support and subscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and canvassing strategy matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The author was advised to make no more applications in person, but carry on the canvass by proxy; prospectuses and bills (even flamboyant ones) were used to announce the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing choices (personal canvassing vs. proxy solicitation, use of prospectuses and bills) affect reception; ill-judged in-person approaches can fail, while proxy canvass and publicity bills can create notice—but publication reliability and content must match promotional promises or trust will be lost.
